🢒 Welcome to Strasbourg!
Explore the various options listed in this university guide based on your profile 
and budget. The toolkit offers plenty of practical advice to help ensure your stay 
goes as smoothly as possible. We hope this practical guide – updated annually 
by the International Relations Office and the Solidarity Mission – answer your 
questions. Please feel free to contact the university for more information.
International Relation Office (Direction des relations internationales)
It welcomes, guides, and supports all international students coming to the University 
of Strasbourg, whether through an inter-university agreement or on an individual 
basis. Integration and cultural events, workshops, assistance with mobility-related 
procedures, and individual appointments are organised by the teams of the 
International Relations Office (DRI) based at the International University House (Maison 
Universitaire Internationale). For further information, students can visit the Maison 
Universitaire Internationale (MUI).
Solidarity Mission (Mission solidarité)
The Solidarity Mission is a service dedicated to all university students. Open from 
Monday to Friday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. It offers listening, support, and personalised 
support throughout the entire administrative process. It also provides drop-in sessions 
with social workers on Tuesdays and Thursdays, without appointment.
↘   47 AVENUE DE LA FORÊT-NOIRE 2ND FLOOR – OFFICE 302 67100 STRASBOURG (TOUT EN MAJUSCULES)  
+33 (0)3 68 85 80 30 | MISSION-SOLIDARITE@UNISTRA.FR | @LAMISSIONSOLIDARITEUNISTRA
International University House (Maison Universitaire Internationale)
Located on the ground floor of the International University House, the Mobility Hub 
is responsible for reception, support, and the promotion of international activities 
within the International Relations Office—as well as the University of Strasbourg’s 
Euraxess Service Centre. These services are dedicated to welcoming international 
visitors and organize workshops to assist foreign students with administrative 
procedures (residence permits, social security, housing search, financial aid), as well 
as French language courses and a cultural calendar . The Euraxess Service Centre offers 
personalised, free assistance specially to international researchers (including PhD 
candidates) and their families.

Beware of scams
This housing guide is intended for informational 
purposes only. It is your responsibility to verify the 
reliability and accuracy of each housing offer . 
Above all, do not pay any money until you have vi-
sited the accommodation or signed a rental contract.
Some landlords ask for a cheque or a bank transfer to reserve accommodation. 
This practice is illegal in France. For advice or legal assistance regarding housing, 
you can contact the ANIL (National Agency for Housing Information) free of charge: 
Q  anil.org. Under no circumstances and for no reason can the University of Stras-
bourg be held responsible for any physical, moral, material, or financial damage 
caused in connection with a rental agreement. In doubt, you can also contact the Ac-
cess to Rights help desk of the Solidarity Mission:° sol-accesauxdroits@unistra.fr

Housing – The 5 main steps to follow
Step 1 | I Start Looking For Accommodation Early Enough
• I look for accommodation and consult the Guide
• I never send money to reserve a place – beware of scams!
• I look for a guarantor
• I carefully plan my move-in expenses (security deposit, insurance, etc.)
Step 2 | I Complete The Administrative Procedures
• I visit the accommodation before signing the contract
• I insure my accommodation
• I sign the lease agreement
• I carry out the move-in inspection (inventory of fixtures)
• I apply for housing assistance with CAF
Step 3 | I Set Up My Utility Accounts
• gas • electricity • internet
Step 4 | I Maintain My Accommodation
• I clean my accommodation regularly
• I avoid waste: I use water and energy responsibly
• I remember to open the windows every day
• I sort my waste
Step 5 | I Move Out Of My Accommodation
• I send my notice on time
• I clean thoroughly and carry out repairs if necessary
• I complete the move-out inspection
• I receive my security deposit
• I report my change of address

Partnership with Studapart
Studapart is a multilingual online 
booking platform that features listings 
from landlords and private university 
residences looking to rent their accommodations to international students.
Thanks to its partnership, the University of Strasbourg offers you special access 
to the platform. You can search for housing and directly contact the landlords or 
private university residences of your choice via the messaging system, and make 
secure reservations on the website. All you need to pay the first month’s rent to 
guarantee your housing reservation. To do so, you will need to provide proof of 
enrollment at the University of Strasbourg (student card, enrollment certificate, 
acceptance letter , or hosting agreement from the laboratory).

Private residences
Private residences are housing facilities managed by independent real estate 
operators. They offer a living environment that combines autonomy and student 
life, offering various amenities such as laundry services, cleaning, and common 
areas to encourage interactions among residents. These establishments are 
often valued for their flexibility and facilities tailored to the needs of students.

Housing expenses
Before coming to Strasbourg, it is very important to prepare your budget 
carefully, as housing is very expensive. 
Here is a list of expenses to plan for:
Costs when moving into your accom-
modation (to be paid during the first 
month):
•   Possible moving costs
•   Possible real estate agency fees: ap -
proximately one month’s rent
•   Security deposit: one month’s rent 
(excluding charges) for unfurnished 
accommodation and two months’ rent 
(excluding charges*) for furnished ac-
commodation
•   First month’s rent
•   Utility set-up fees: water , gas, electri-
city, internet
•   Home insurance: mandatory
Monthly expenses:
•   Internet subscription
•   Utilities: water , electricity and gas
Average monthly rent estimates:
•   University residence (Crous): between 
€201 and €600
•   Private student residence: between 
€520 and €650
•   Studio in the private sector: between 
€500 and €750, charges included
Warning!
Do not pay reservation cheques 
or other illegal fees.
This is prohibited by law, even 
if some agencies ask for them!
Be cautious when looking for 
accommodation. Do not pay 
reservation fees or any other 
unjustified fees. 
Such fees are prohibited by 
French law, even if some agen
cies or landlords ask for them. 
If in doubt, seek advice from 
your host institution before 
making any payment.
* Note: charges are the common buil-
ding expenses and may sometimes in-
clude water , heating or other utilities, 
depending on the accommodation.
The little dictionary about housing
You are looking for accommodation, but the vocabulary and abbreviations used 
in housing advertisements can be difficult to understand. Here is a glossary to 
help you:
Home insurance
This mandatory insurance covers da-
mage that may occur in your accom-
modation (such as water leaks or fires). 
You can obtain it from an insurance 
company, a bank, or a student mutual 
organisation.
 Lease or rental agreement
This is a written document signed 
between the tenant (you) and the lan-
dlord. It states the rights and responsi-
bilities of both parties: duration of the 
rental, rent, charges, notice period, se-
curity deposit, etc. In shared accommo-
dation, there may be a single lease for 
all tenants or several individual leases. 
Be careful: a lease may contain unfair 
clauses, so take the time to read it be-
fore signing. 
Termination or ending of the lease
You can terminate your lease by res-
pecting the required notice period and 
informing your landlord by registered 
letter .
Monthly service charges
These are fees related to the mainte -
nance of common areas (such as the 
elevator or cleaning). They may be in -
cluded in the rent or listed separately. 
Do not confuse them with personal 
utility bills such as water , electricity or 
gas.
Shared accommodation
Living in a property with other people 
(roommates). There are two main types 
of leases: a single contract signed by all 
tenants with a solidarity clause, or indi-
vidual leases for each tenant without a 
solidarity clause.
In shared accommodation a solidarity 
clause means that all tenants are joint-
ly responsible for paying the rent and 
charges. If one tenant does not pay, the 
landlord can ask the other tenants to 
cover the missing amount.
 Security deposit (“caution”)
This is an amount of money paid to the 
landlord when signing the contract. It is 
returned within two months after you 
leave, unless damage is found.

Pratical guides

W ARNING: Rental scams are common!
Some individuals pretend to be landlords in order to extort money 
or identity documents.
How can you spot a suspicious 
listing?
Certain warning signs should alert you, 
such as an unusually low rent, identi-
cal descriptions appearing in multiple 
advertisements, or photos copied from 
other listings. 
If a private landlord asks you to transfer 
money through services such as Mo -
neyGram or Western Union, refuse!
Finally, if you go through a real estate 
agency, keep in mind that agency fees 
cannot be requested before the lease is 
signed. If someone asks you for money 
in exchange for property viewings or 
lists of accommodations, be cautious 
and do not proceed.
If you have been the victim of a rental 
scam or believe that a listing may be 
fraudulent, report it without delay at 
internet-signalement.gouv.fr
How to prepare your rental application file
The landlord or the real estate agent may ask you to provide documents to 
verify your identity and your financial situation. This allows them to check the 
reliability of your application. Here are the main documents you should prepare 
that they may request:
 Identity document
This can be an identity card, a passport, a driver’s license, or a valid residence 
permit.
Proof of professional or student status
This can be an employment contract, an employer certificate, an internship agree-
ment, a student card or certificate of enrolment, as well as any recent document 
showing your professional activity.
 Proof of financial resources
If you receive a scholarship, you will need to provide proof of it. If you are employed, 
you must provide your last three payslips. If you receive financial support from your 
family, you will need to show proof of the amount and the regularity of this support.
Proof of address
This can be a rent receipt, an electricity bill, a certificate of residence, or a sworn 
statement from the person hosting you.
Copy of your latest tax notice
Even if you are a foreign student, some landlords may ask for your latest tax notice. 
If you do not have one, they may accept a tax notice from your parents or guarantor .

GOOD TO KNOW! 
French law forbids landlords from requesting certain confidential 
documents, such as bank statements, bank account certificates, 
marriage contracts, medical records, etc.
Discrimination in access to housing is also prohibited. A landlord cannot 
refuse an application on the basis of origin, religion, political opinions, 
gender , physical appearance, etc. It is common for landlords to ask 
for a guarantor , that is, a person who agrees to pay your rent if you are 
unable to do so. In France, guarantors are almost always required, whether 
you are a foreigner or French.
If you do not have a guarantor ,  
do not worry—there are alternatives:
VISALE
A free guarantee scheme that covers rent and charges in 
case of unpaid rent. More information at visale.fr.
LOCAP ASS
A free service that can advance or pay the security de -
posit. More information at locapass.actionlogement.fr.
The rental agreement
What is a rental contract? A rental contract, also called a lease agreement, is an 
agreement to rent a property between the landlord and the tenant.
The rental contract must be written, dated, and signed by both the landlord and 
the tenant. Each person must keep an identical copy of the lease and the signed 
documents.
The rental contract must include 
the following information:
•   Name and address of the landlord
•   Names of the tenants (if it is shared 
accommodation)
•   Start date and duration of the lease
•   Purpose of the accommodation (main 
residence or temporary stay)
•   Living area in square meters
•   Description of the accommodation 
(house or apartment, number of 
rooms) and equipment
•   Amount of the security deposit
•   Amount of agency fees (if applicable)
•   Rent and charges (amounts and pay-
ment dates)
Focus: The security deposit
The security deposit is a sum 
of money that the tenant must 
pay to the landlord when 
signing the lease. This money 
is collected and kept by the 
landlord during the entire 
rental period. It guarantees 
that you will take care of 
the accommodation and covers 
possible damages.
Maximum amount:
•   One month’s rent (excluding charges) 
for unfurnished accommodation
•   Up to two month’s rent for furnished 
accommodation
40  •           • 41
Pratical guides

What does the security deposit 
cover?
The security deposit can be used to co-
ver:
•   Unpaid rent or charges at the end of 
the rental period
•   The cost of repairs and damages
•   Lack of proper maintenance of the 
accommodation
•   Cleaning costs if the accommodation 
is not left in an acceptable condition
If damages are found when you leave 
the accommodation, the cost will be 
deducted from the security deposit. 
The remaining amount (or the full 
deposit if there is no damage) must 
be returned to you no later than two 
months after your departure.
Warning!
Some clauses are forbidden by law in a lease, such as:
•   Requiring payment of rent exclusively by direct debit
•   Forcing the tenant to subscribe to a specific insurance policy
•   Allowing the landlord to reduce or remove services mentioned in the contract 
without equivalent compensation
•   Holding the tenant responsible for all damage to the accommodation even when 
they are not responsible for it
•   Preventing the tenant from holding the landlord responsible or exempting the 
landlord from all responsibility
•   Forbidding the tenant from hosting people who do not usually live with them
•   Forbidding the tenant from taking part in political, trade union, association, or 
religious activities
Good to know! 
The rent may be revised once per year , but only if the contract specifies it.
Where can I find the detailed regulations?
Legal text: Law n° 89-462 of 6 July 1989.
Your Rights and Obligations
Landlord’s obligations
Provide decent housing
The landlord must ensure that the ac -
commodation is in good condition and 
suitable to live in.
Comply with legal housing 
standards
The accommodation must meet legal 
living standards, with electrical and 
heating systems that meet safety re -
gulations:
•   minimum surface area and energy 
performance
•   no risk to the tenant’s safety or health
•   no pests or infestations
•   provision of certain basic facilities 
(drinking water , heating, etc.)
Provide a rent receipt
Upon request, the landlord must provi-
de a rent receipt free of charge. 
Tenant’s obligations
Pay rent and charges
The tenant must pay the rent and 
charges on the agreed dates.
Home insurance
The tenant must take out home insu-
rance covering rental risks.
Carry out certain maintenance work
The tenant must take care of minor 
maintenance that is not the landlord’s 
responsibility, such as small repairs or 
boiler maintenance.
Maintain the accommodation
The tenant must keep the accommoda-
tion clean and in good condition.
Respect the neighbors
The tenant must avoid causing noise or 
disturbances to neighbors.
Do not sublet without permission
The tenant cannot sublet the accommo-
dation without landlord’s consent.
In case of a dispute
If a problem occurs, first try to resolve it amicably by discussing it with the 
other party. If this does not work, you can seek advice from the National 
Agency for Housing Information (Anil) or contact the Departmental Agency 
for Housing Information (Adil) near you. For more information, consult the 
website of Adil Bas-Rhin: adil67.org
Additional information is also available on service-public.fr.

 ▢  I carry out a detailed inventory and condition report with the landlord (known as 
a “joint inspection”); it is signed by both the landlord and myself
 ▢  I record the water , gas, and electricity meter readings when move-in and move-
out
 ▢  I open electricity and gas accounts (unless they are included in the charges)
 ▢  If necessary, I take out an internet subscription
 ▢  I remember to notify my change of address: university, bank, insurance, tax 
office, CAF (family benefits office), social security, prefecture
Did you know?
The security deposit is kept by the landlord for the entire duration of the tenancy 
and may be deposited or cashed upon receipt. It cannot be considered as an advance 
on rent, and I must continue paying rent until the official move-out date.
The inventory and condition report is a mandatory document describing the condi-
tion of the accommodation room by room, as well as its equipment. It helps prevent 
disputes when moving out.
It must be detailed: room by room, from floor to ceiling. All equipment must be 
described: cupboards, heating, shower , type and condition of wall coverings, doors, 
windows, shutters, etc.
Electricity and Gas
To open an electricity or gas account (very quick process), you will need your lease 
agreement, an ID document, and the name of the previous account holder .
Can a landlord keep a duplicate set of keys to a tenant’s 
accommodation?
Yes, the landlord may keep a duplicate set of keys to the property they 
rent out. However , they are not allowed to enter the accommodation 
without the tenant’s consent. Even in case of emergency (for example,
water damage), the landlord must obtain the tenant’s permission before 
entering. If the landlord enters without the tenant’s consent, 
the tenant can file a complaint for unlawful entry.

when you leave. It is your responsibility to maintain it regularly and return it

The sink, shower , and toilet. Also keep

Moving Out of Your Accommodation
Move-out Checklist:
 ▢  I inform the landlord of my departure (notice period)
 ▢  I transfer or cancel my home insurance
 ▢  I transfer or cancel my electricity/gas/water/internet/phone subscriptions
 ▢  I empty the accommodation and make sure to clean every corner: cupboards, 
ventilation system, electrical outlets, windows, appliances if provided, etc.
 ▢  I check that doors, cupboards, windows, switches, etc. are working properly. All 
these details will help you avoid deductions from your security deposit
 ▢  I carry out minor repairs (filling holes, small paint touch-ups, etc.). All these 
details will help you avoid deductions from your security deposit
 ▢  I complete the move-out inspection with the landlord and return the keys
 ▢  I provide my new address to the former landlord to ensure a quick return of the 
security deposit (usually within 1 month)
 ▢  I inform relevant organisations of my change of address: prefecture (ANEF), tax 
office, family allowance office (CAF), health insurance office (CPAM), etc.
Did you know?
Notice period
You can leave your accommodation at any time, but you must respect a notice period 
and pay rent during this time.
•   Notice period for an unfurnished rental agreement: 3 months (often 1 month in 
Strasbourg)
•   Notice period for a furnished rental agreement or a mobility lease: one month
